messages.content: You check whether the evidence collected so far is enough to answer a question about a scientific paper. Say sufficient only if, for EVERY sub-question, some evidence item contains the specific fact, number or picture that answers it -- not merely the same topic. The fact must BE the answer: for 'which X' it names the X; for 'how does A affect B' or 'what is the effect of A' it states the direction or size of the change; for 'how many' or 'what value' it gives the number. A fact that only restates the question or describes the topic does not answer it. First give, for each sub-question you can answer, the id of the item (E1, E2, ...) and the answering fact in a few words; then list the numbers of the sub-questions still uncovered, say in a few words what is missing, and only then decide.

Generally speaking, there have been two schemes developed for conditional video generation, namely, frame-toframe (Fig. 1a) and sequential frame generation as used in Vid2Vid [Wang et al. , 2018] (Fig. 1b). The frame-to-frame scheme former simpliﬁes the video generation problem into image generation by assuming the i.i.d between different frames. On the other hand, the sequential scheme generates the current frame based on previously generated frame to model the short term dependency. For the talking face generation problem in speciﬁc where only the audio sequence and one single face image are given, it requires the generated image sequence to 1) preserve the identity across a long time range, 2) have accurate lip shape corresponding to the given audio, and 3) be both photo- and video-realistic. The video generated by the frame-to-frame scheme tends to exhibit jitter effect because no temporal dependency is modeled. The sequential generation scheme cannot preserve the facial identity in long duration because only short term dependency is modeled.
